The Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) sets thresholds for weekly influenza-like
illness (ILI) or acute respiratory infection (ARI) rates from past seasons
[@vega2013]. This chapter follows its steps one by one, with a figure for each
step. The data are weekly ILI consultation rates per 100,000 in Croatia, week 26
of 2022 to week 43 of 2026, from ECDC's European Respiratory Virus Surveillance
Summary (ERVISS) [@ecdc_erviss]. In each figure, point at a blue symbol in a
formula to see where it is in the chart.

## The method in brief {#sec-mem-brief}

MEM uses past seasons to set thresholds for the next season. It works in three
steps.

1. **Find the epidemic weeks.** For each past season, the MAP curve gives the
   length and the timing of the epidemic. This splits the season into three
   periods: pre-epidemic, epidemic and post-epidemic.
2. **Set the epidemic threshold.** From each pre-epidemic period, take the $n$
   highest weekly rates, where $n = 30 / \text{number of seasons}$. Pool these
   values from all seasons. The epidemic threshold is their mean plus
   $z_{0.05}$ standard deviations, where $z_{0.05} = 1.645$. A post-epidemic
   threshold comes from the post-epidemic periods in the same way.
3. **Set the intensity thresholds.** From each epidemic period, take the $n$
   highest weekly rates and pool them. Their geometric mean and upper limits
   give the thresholds for the levels of intensity.

In a new season, the first weekly rate above the epidemic threshold signals the
start of the epidemic. The intensity thresholds then give the level of each
week.

> The purpose of the MEM is to model influenza epidemics based upon historical
> data from a specific country or region. The method has three main steps:
> First, the length, start and the end of the annual epidemics are determined,
> splitting the season in three periods: a pre-epidemic, an epidemic and a
> post-epidemic period. Secondly, the baseline and the epidemic thresholds are
> calculated using the pre-epidemic and post-epidemic values of historical
> seasons. Finally, thresholds for different levels of intensity are computed.
> [@vega2013]

## The data: one row per season {#sec-mem-data}

> Weekly rates were estimated at least for 33 weeks in every season, from week
> 40 of 1 year to the week 20 of the following year. [@vega2013]

> Missing values in weekly rates at the beginning or at the end of the
> surveillance period did not affect the method and were excluded from
> calculations. Missing weekly data during the surveillance period were imputed
> with a smooth regression over the full season's data using a small window
> parameter. [@vega2013]

A real series needs this preparation. Some weeks were never reported, some
weeks fall between seasons, and the current season is not finished. The paper
used countries with five or more seasons of data [@vega2013]. ERVISS has four
complete seasons for Croatia, so the numbers in this chapter are a worked
example, not Croatia's official thresholds.

::: {#fig-mem-series}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-mem-series" class="mem-fig"></div>
```

Weekly ILI rates in Croatia as reported to ERVISS. Hatching marks weeks with no
data; a week with no data is not a week with zero cases. Brackets mark the four
complete seasons. Press **Cut into seasons**: the weeks between seasons and the
unfinished current season are left out. One week inside a season has no data,
week 19 of 2025. It is filled with a smoothing regression over the season, as
in the authors' R package [@lozano_mem]; the regression gives a value below 0,
so the week is set to 0.
:::

## Step 1: the epidemic period of each season {#sec-mem-step1}

> In the first step, for each season separately, the length of the epidemic
> period is estimated as the minimum number of consecutive weeks with the
> maximum accumulated rates percentage (MAP). [@vega2013]

> The MAP curve draws the maximum cumulated rate for a period of a given length
> $r$, expressed as percentage of the total rate of the $j$th season.
> [@vega2013]

::: {#fig-mem-map}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-mem-map" class="mem-fig"></div>
```

The best window of $r$ weeks in every season, beside the MAP curves. For each
number of weeks $r$, the window of $r$ consecutive weeks is placed where its total is largest, so it can be in a
different place in each season.
:::

> Then the MAP curve is smoothed, using a smoothing regression (over $r$),
> selecting automatically the window parameter. The optimum number of weeks for
> each season is determined calculating the increment in the percentage from
> one number of weeks to the next one. &hellip; When this increment is lower
> than the predefined criteria, the optimum is found. [@vega2013]

The criterion is $\delta$. It depends on the country, ranges from 2% to 4% and
is chosen to maximise sensitivity and specificity [@vega2013]. Once the optimum
number of weeks $r^*$ is found, the epidemic starts at week $k^*$, the first
week of the window of $r^*$ weeks with the largest total. The weeks before the
epidemic are the pre-epidemic period, and the weeks after it are the
post-epidemic period [@vega2013].

::: {#fig-mem-opt}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-mem-opt" class="mem-fig"></div>
```

Left: the MAP curve of one season and its smoothed version. Right: the
increment in the percentage from one number of weeks to the next. When the
increment is lower than $\delta$, the optimum length $r^*$ is found. Bottom:
the best window of $r^*$ weeks starts at week $k^*$; the epidemic runs from
week $k^*$ to week $k^* + r^* - 1$, and this splits every season into three
periods.
:::

## Step 2: the epidemic threshold {#sec-mem-step2}

> In the second step, the baseline and threshold using pre-epidemic values of
> historical seasons are calculated. The baseline is the arithmetic mean of all
> pre-epidemic rates of all historical seasons (pooled together as a single
> sample). [@vega2013]

> To calculate the threshold, only a set of pre-epidemic values is considered.
> For each season, the highest $n$ values from the pre-epidemic period are
> taken, where $n$ = 30/number of seasons. [@vega2013]

> With all these $n \times N$ values, a one-tailed point 95% confidence
> interval is calculated. &hellip; The upper limit of the confidence interval is
> the epidemic threshold. Additionally, a post-epidemic threshold is calculated
> using the same procedure. [@vega2013]

So the epidemic threshold is $t^* = \bar{t} + z_{0.05} \times S_t$, where
$\bar{t}$ and $S_t$ are the mean and the standard deviation of the
$n \times N$ values, and $z_{0.05} = 1.645$. With four seasons,
$n = 30 / 4 = 7.5$, which the authors' R package rounds to 8 [@lozano_mem], so
32 values are pooled.

::: {.callout-note}

$z_{0.05}$ is the point of the standard normal curve with 5% of the area above
it. Its value is 1.645.

The calculation assumes that the pooled values come from a normal distribution
with their mean and standard deviation. In any normal distribution, 95% of the
values lie below the mean plus $z_{0.05}$ standard deviations, and 5% lie above
it.

The interval is one-tailed because only high rates matter for an alarm, so all
of the 5% is in the upper tail. A two-tailed 95% interval would put 2.5% in
each tail and use $z_{0.025} = 1.96$ instead.

The interval is a *point* interval: it is for one weekly value, not for the
mean. So it uses the standard deviation, not the standard error. In plain
words, if the highest pre-epidemic weeks of a new season follow the same
distribution as in past seasons, about 1 in 20 of them would still be above the
threshold.
:::

::: {#fig-mem-threshold}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-mem-threshold" class="mem-fig"></div>
```

Top: every season, zoomed in on its pre-epidemic weeks; its $n$ highest weeks
are dark teal, with their rates per 100,000. Bottom left: the same $n \times N$
values side by side. Bottom right: their histogram on its side, so that it
shares the rate axis with the bars, with the normal curve of the same mean,
standard deviation and area. The $z$ axis on the right counts standard
deviations from the mean. The threshold $t^*$ is one horizontal line across
both panels, at $z_{0.05}$ on the $z$ axis, with 5% of the curve's area above
it. Press **Show how** to watch the steps in order, and **t\* on the seasons**
to draw the threshold on every season.
:::

## Step 3: the intensity thresholds {#sec-mem-step3}

> Thresholds for different levels of intensity are calculated using the $n$
> highest values of each epidemic period to build a sample of $n \times N$
> rates. With the sample, the geometric mean and 50%, 90% and 95% one-sided
> confidence intervals are calculated. These upper limits are the threshold for
> the different levels of intensity of the epidemic. [@vega2013]

As in step 2, $z_\alpha$ is the point of the standard normal curve with
$\alpha$ of the area above it. Step 3 uses it on the logarithms of the rates:
$z_{0.50} = 0$ for the 50% limit, which is the geometric mean itself,
$z_{0.10} = 1.282$ for the 90% limit and $z_{0.05} = 1.645$ for the 95% limit.
The three thresholds split the weekly rates into five levels: baseline, low,
medium, high and very high [@vega2015]. The paper says countries may change
these percentages [@vega2013]. @vega2015 and the authors' R package
[@lozano_mem] use 40%, 90% and 97.5%.

::: {#fig-mem-intensity}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-mem-intensity" class="mem-fig"></div>
```

Top: every season, zoomed in on its epidemic weeks; its $n$ highest weeks are
dark blue, with their rates. Bottom: the same values side by side, and their
histogram on its side, on a log axis. The normal curve of the logs is centred
on the geometric mean ($z = 0$); the 90% and 95% limits are at $z_{0.10}$ and
$z_{0.05}$ on the $z$ axis. So the three thresholds split the curve's area into
50%, 40%, 5% and 5%. Switch to the rate scale to see the same values and the
same curve on the rates. Press **I50, I90, I95 on the seasons** to draw the
thresholds on every season.
:::

## Step 4: watching a new season {#sec-mem-step4}

> The main purpose of the method is to define the baseline influenza activity
> in historical data and to establish an epidemic threshold above which the
> weekly rates are considered to be in the epidemic period. [@vega2013]

> Rates in the pre-epidemic period were expected to be lower than the
> pre-epidemic threshold rate, while rates within the epidemic period are
> expected to be higher. Finally, rates in the post-epidemic period were
> expected to be lower than the post-epidemic threshold rate. [@vega2013]

The paper calls the first week with a rate above the epidemic threshold the
alert week [@vega2013]. During the epidemic, the intensity thresholds give the
level of each week. The paper gives no rule for the end of the epidemic in a
new season; the authors' R package ends it at the first week after the peak
with a rate below the post-epidemic threshold [@lozano_mem].

> If influenza weekly epidemiological data are accompanied by timely virological
> data, virus circulation should be taken into account to make appropriate
> public health decisions. [@vega2013]

@fig-mem-monitor starts with the current season, 2026/27, and the thresholds
from all four past seasons. The data end in week 43 of 2026. To show how a
season reaches the threshold, the weeks after that are illustrative, not data:
each one is the average rate of the four past seasons in the same week.

::: {#fig-mem-monitor}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-mem-monitor" class="mem-fig"></div>
```

Press **Play** to add the weeks one by one. Solid bars are data and outlined
bars are illustrative; the colour of a bar gives its level. At the right, step
3's curve of past epidemic weeks stands on its side, cut at the intensity
thresholds. Choose a past season to replay it, as in the paper's
cross-validation below.
:::

> For each country, each single season was extracted from the historical
> records to be used as the target season. MEM calculated the beginning and the
> end of the epidemic period of the target season. On the basis of the
> remaining seasons, excluding the target season, MEM calculated the pre- and
> post-epidemic thresholds. [@vega2013]

In a replay, the band under the chart is the epidemic period that step 1 finds
for the target season, and the reading scores the alert with the paper's
timeliness, detection lag and false alerts.

## Notes {#sec-mem-notes}

- The paper gives step 3 in words. The formulas in @fig-mem-intensity are how
  the authors' R package computes it [@lozano_mem].
- The MAP curve is smoothed by a local linear kernel regression with the window
  chosen by AICc. The results were checked against R's `sm` package.
- The data are the ERVISS snapshot of 30 October 2026, released under the EUPL
  1.2 licence [@ecdc_erviss].
